StrikeShark persistence: Run key / scheduled task launching SystemSettings.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the StrikeShark persistence mechanism where a Registry Run key (or scheduled task) is configured to relaunch the side-loaded SystemSettings.exe at logon or on a schedule. Legitimate autostart entries never reference SystemSettings.exe, making this a high-fidelity persistence signal. Rationale: Combines the article's named persistence vectors (Run keys + scheduled tasks relaunching SystemSettings.exe) with the path-anomaly filter; legitimate software never autostarts the OS SystemSettings binary from a non-System32 location. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://gbhackers.com/sharkloader-malware-to-deploy-cobalt-strike/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom IT scripts that pin a Settings shortcut to autostart (rare, and usually point to the System32 binary)
  • OEM utilities referencing 'SystemSettings' branding in a value name
  • Group Policy logon scripts that legitimately invoke ms-settings: URIs (these reference the URI, not the exe)
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full RegistryValueData to confirm it launches SystemSettings.exe from a writable path. 2) Contain: remove the Run-key value / disable the scheduled task, then isolate the host and quarantine the binary set. 3) Hunt: enumerate all autoruns on the host, check for additional scheduled tasks running 'even if no user is logged in', and sweep the estate for the same value-data string.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "SystemSettings.exe"
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Windows\System32")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "CurrentVersion\\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "SystemSettings.exe"
| where RegistryValueData !has "\\Windows\\System32"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharkLoader / dropper known-bad MD5 execution (StrikeShark) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on execution or file-write of any of the nine SharkLoader / dropper samples published for the StrikeShark campaign, including droppers masquerading as Google Update and Cisco AnyConnect installers. Pure IOC match across process, file and image-load telemetry. Rationale: Direct match on the nine MD5 IOCs Kaspersky published for SharkLoader and its Google-Update / Cisco-AnyConnect-themed droppers; hash equality is zero-ambiguity once corroborated by the vendor report. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://www.cryptika.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures-to-drop-sharkloader-malware/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform replaying samples in a monitored detonation VM
  • Reverse engineer analysing the sample on a corporate workstation
  • Hash collision is not a realistic FP for MD5 at this scale but legacy AV test corpora may carry the file
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not a sandbox/RE host) and capture the file path and parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the sample, and block the hashes org-wide via custom indicators. 3) Hunt: pivot to the side-load, persistence and C2 UCs on the affected host and any host that received the same installer-themed lure.

StrikeShark Cobalt Strike C2 beacon to Microsoft-lookalike domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts beaconing to the four Microsoft-impersonating C2 domains used by StrikeShark to front Cobalt Strike (connect-microsoft.com, ms-record.com, ms-record.top, ms-tray.top). Catches both DNS resolution and outbound connections to the lookalike infrastructure. Rationale: Matches the four named StrikeShark C2 domains directly; the Microsoft-lookalike naming (connect-microsoft, ms-record, ms-tray) means any internal resolution is high-fidelity malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://gbhackers.com/sharkloader-malware-to-deploy-cobalt-strike/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the sample on a monitored host generating the lookup
  • Threat-intel scanner / sinkhole probing the domains from a corporate range
  • Typo-driven user navigation to connect-microsoft.com (rare, still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection (expect SystemSettings.exe or a beacon-injected process). 2) Contain: sinkhole/block all four domains at the resolver and proxy, isolate the resolving host. 3) Hunt: pivot on resolved IPs to find other internal hosts beaconing to the same infrastructure, and correlate with the side-load and component-drop UCs on each.

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("connect-microsoft.com","ms-record.com","ms-record.top","ms-tray.top")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName, Result, RemoteIp
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StrikeShark post-exploitation recon tooling (FScan / Searchall / Pillager) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of the open-source reconnaissance and credential-harvesting tools StrikeShark deploys after foothold: FScan (network scan), Searchall and Pillager (data/credential collection). Matches on both binary names and command-line tokens. Rationale: Uses the three specific tool names Kaspersky attributes to StrikeShark's recon phase (FScan, Searchall, Pillager) — commodity tools, hence Medium confidence, but the trio together on one host post-foothold is a strong campaign indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/
ATT&CKT1046 T1087.002 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / pentest engagement legitimately running FScan or Pillager
  • A sysadmin tool or filename containing the token 'searchall' (e.g. a search utility) tripping the cmdline match
  • Security testing scripts referencing 'fscan' in arguments
  • Software named 'Pillager' unrelated to the collector
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cb.exe","cobaltstrike.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "redteam"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the tool is not an authorised red-team asset (check change/engagement tickets), review the command line for scan targets or output paths. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the tool binary and its output files, and rotate credentials for any account exposed by Pillager/Searchall. 3) Hunt: pivot to LSASS/NTDS credential-theft activity and AD enumeration from the same host, and check which internal ranges FScan touched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("fscan.exe","searchall.exe","pillager.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fscan","searchall","pillager")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("fscan.exe","searchall.exe","pillager.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("fscan","searchall","pillager")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StrikeShark initial access: public-facing server process spawning shell (web shell) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the StrikeShark initial-access pattern where an exploited internet-facing service (Exchange/IIS w3wp.exe, Openfire/GeoServer java.exe, Apache httpd.exe) spawns a command shell or the campaign's SystemSettings.exe via a deployed web shell. Maps to the ProxyLogon/Openfire/GeoServer exploitation chain described in the article. Rationale: Targets the article's stated initial-access vector (ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855, Openfire CVE-2023-32315, GeoServer CVE-2024-36401 → web shell), pivoting on the server processes that host those apps spawning shells or the campaign-specific SystemSettings.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/strikeshark-campaign/120326/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-cisco-anyconnect-and-google-update-lures/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Exchange/SharePoint health probes or admin scripts where w3wp legitimately invokes cmd/powershell
  • Java application servers shelling out for legitimate maintenance jobs
  • Monitoring agents that spawn net.exe/whoami.exe under a web service account
  • Patch/deployment tooling running under the IIS app pool identity
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","SCOM","MonitoringHost") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the child command line and the web-root for recently written .aspx/.jsp/.war files (web shell). 2) Contain: isolate the server, take the web app offline or remove the web shell, and reset the service-account and any harvested credentials. 3) Hunt: confirm the exploited CVE via app/IIS logs, then pivot to SharkLoader side-load, persistence and C2 UCs and check for the named recon tools.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","SystemSettings.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\SystemSettings.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\w3wp.exe OR *\W3WP.exe OR *\java.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\httpd.exe OR *\UMWorkerProcess.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\SystemSettings.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\net.exe OR *\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(w3wp|java|httpd|UMWorkerProcess)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|systemsettings|whoami|net|net1|cscript)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe")) (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","SystemSettings.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("w3wp.exe","java.exe","httpd.exe","UMWorkerProcess.exe")) (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","SystemSettings.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","cscript.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("connect-microsoft.com", "ms-record.com", "ms-record.top", "ms-tray.top")

let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    product: windows

    selection_domain:

            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2021-26855", "CVE-2023-32315", "CVE-2024-36401", "CVE-2016-4437", "CVE-2021-36260", "CVE-2021-27076", "CVE-2022-27925", "CVE-2022-41082", "CVE-2023-46747", "CVE-2024-21762", "CVE-2025-55182", "CVE-2022-40684", "CVE-2023-20198")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or SHA1 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b") or MD5 in~ ("c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c559cc68986933200fd5d9e4388e2f58", "b3352b42432dedc4a519f011dc8b5d5a", "24fcebdeecba65004fdb0923763d74fd", "9c872a0d5d5a38950e8b9ac9b488be3f", "aa3086be652c8b20b0b29b2730d57119", "a514d1bb62d7916475946fe7c07ac0aa", "9cbd560f820c95d7c38342cd558cb5c6", "d98f568496512e4f98670c61c97cb07a", "1f65544978b8ea0e745e573b8ee9684b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound OpenAI org-invite email from noreply@tm.openai.com impersonating own company · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Employee clicked OpenAI org-invite accept link from fraudulent tenant invite · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process

Inbound OpenAI org-invite email from noreply@tm.openai.com impersonating own company AIDelivery High
Hunts the Push Security 'Poisoned Tenant' campaign: legitimate OpenAI notification emails (noreply@tm.openai.com) inviting employees into an attacker-created ChatGPT/OpenAI organization named after the target company. Because the mail genuinely originates from OpenAI infrastructure and passes SPF/DKIM/DMARC, normal email security lets it through — this surfaces every such invite for analyst triage against whether the org is company-sanctioned. Rationale: Uses the verbatim sender noreply@tm.openai.com and the fixed OpenAI invite subject template 'You were invited to the organization <X> on OpenAI' both read directly from the invite screenshot (image [3]) and confirmed across SCWorld/TechRadar write-ups. The sender genuinely passes auth, so the subject template + inbound direction is the only reliable mail-side anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cybersecurity-firms-targeted-by-fraudulent-openai-organization-invites/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/openai-team-invitation-system-exploited-in-sophisticated-phishing-scam • https://www.techradar.com/pro/beware-hackers-have-hijacked-openais-invite-your-team-feature-to-break-into-your-business • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/o/openai/fake-organization-tenants/push-openai-invite.jpg
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Company has sanctioned ChatGPT Team/Enterprise and IT legitimately invites staff into the corporate OpenAI org
  • A developer or colleague on a Gmail-linked OpenAI account legitimately invites a teammate to a shared OpenAI API org
  • A partner/vendor genuinely invites your staff to a joint OpenAI project workspace
  • Security researcher intentionally accepting an invite to investigate (as Push's own researcher did)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the named organization is a company-sanctioned OpenAI/ChatGPT tenant. Open the raw email and check the inviter's email domain in the body — a free-mail (gmail.com) inviter whose org name equals your company is the malicious tell; OpenAI itself flags 'inviter's email domain does not match your domain'. 2) Contain: instruct recipients NOT to click 'Accept invite'; if any already joined, have them leave the org and rotate any credentials/secrets pasted into ChatGPT; report the fraudulent org to OpenAI. 3) Hunt: pull every recipient of the same NetworkMessageId/subject across the tenant, check UrlClickEvents for who clicked the accept link, and review whether targeted users are high-value (research, exec, security) consistent with the campaign's reconnaissance.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromAddress =~ "noreply@tm.openai.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "tm.openai.com"
| where Subject contains "invited to the organization" and Subject contains "on OpenAI"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

Employee clicked OpenAI org-invite accept link from fraudulent tenant invite AIExploitation Medium
Correlates the OpenAI invite email (noreply@tm.openai.com) to a Safe Links click on its 'Accept invite' URL, surfacing employees who actually engaged with a potentially attacker-created OpenAI organization. A click means the user is about to join a tenant where any data entered into ChatGPT prompts is harvestable by the attacker. Rationale: Joins the campaign invite (verbatim noreply@tm.openai.com sender + 'invited to the organization' subject) to UrlClickEvents on NetworkMessageId, so it fires only when a real user clicked the OpenAI accept link — the moment passive delivery becomes active engagement. ClickedThrough/IsClickedThrough flags a user who bypassed any warning. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cybersecurity-firms-targeted-by-fraudulent-openai-organization-invites/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/openai-team-invitation-system-exploited-in-sophisticated-phishing-scam • https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/o/openai/fake-organization-tenants/push-openai-invite.jpg
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User clicks an invite to a genuinely company-sanctioned OpenAI org
  • Safe Links detonation/pre-fetch registering as a click rather than a real human click
  • User clicks to investigate/report the suspicious invite (security-aware behavior)
  • Legitimate developer accepting a real shared OpenAI API org invite from a colleague
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the AccountUpn who clicked and confirm whether the linked OpenAI organization is corporate-approved; check if ActionType is ClickedThrough (user bypassed a warning) for higher priority. 2) Contain: contact the user, confirm whether they joined/authenticated to the org, and if so have them leave the org and rotate any secrets or source code that may have been pasted into the workspace; force re-auth on their OpenAI/ChatGPT sessions. 3) Hunt: enumerate all other recipients of the same invite who also appear in UrlClickEvents, and review those users' subsequent network traffic to openai.com/chatgpt.com for evidence of data submission into the attacker tenant.
let Invites = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where SenderFromAddress =~ "noreply@tm.openai.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "tm.openai.com"
    | where Subject contains "invited to the organization"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTime = Timestamp;
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| join kind=inner Invites on NetworkMessageId
| project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, EmailTime, NetworkMessageId
| order by ClickTime desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Invites = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where SenderFromAddress =~ "noreply@tm.openai.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "tm.openai.com"
    | where Subject contains "invited to the organization"
    | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTime = TimeGenerated;
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| join kind=inner Invites on NetworkMessageId
| project ClickTime = TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, EmailTime, NetworkMessageId
| order by ClickTime desc
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

TinyRCT AppDomainManager injection via chrome_setup.exe loading MyAppDomainManager.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 .NET AppDomainManager hijack where a legitimate signed chrome_setup.exe is forced (via chrome_setup.exe.config) to load the rogue MyAppDomainManager.dll, which acts as a downloader. Article-specific because the bespoke DLL/config filenames are unique to this campaign's loader. Rationale: Pivots on the campaign-unique filenames MyAppDomainManager.dll and chrome_setup.exe.config named directly by Unit 42 and cross-confirmed in their technical report; AppDomainManager hijack of a signed binary is near-zero in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cl-sta-1062-hackers-use-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1574.014 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Visual Studio / .NET SDK developers using legitimately named AppDomainManager assemblies during local debugging
  • Internal .NET applications that legitimately ship a custom AppDomainManager via app.config (rare in enterprise endpoints)
  • Security tooling that loads instrumentation DLLs with similar naming conventions
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools that emit a transient .exe.config alongside an installer
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\dotnet\sdk\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process path/signature of chrome_setup.exe and the load location of MyAppDomainManager.dll; pull the DLL SHA256 and detonate/VT it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, and quarantine MyAppDomainManager.dll and chrome_setup.exe.config; block outbound to 139.180.134.221. 3) Hunt: search the host for PerfWatson2.exe drops and outbound connections to 45.32.113.172, and sweep the fleet for the same DLL/config filenames.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "MyAppDomainManager.dll"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DllName=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("MyAppDomainManager.dll","chrome_setup.exe.config")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX web shell execution: IIS w3wp.exe spawning shell/recon child processes AIInstallation High
Detects CL-STA-1062's ASPX web-shell foothold by flagging the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning command shells or recon LOLBins. Article-specific to the initial-access vector where web shells facilitate recon and outbound callbacks from compromised internet-facing servers. Rationale: Uses the article's stated initial-access vector (ASPX web shells on internet-facing servers driving recon/outbound callbacks) expressed as the high-fidelity w3wp.exe→shell/recon process-tree pivot; legitimate IIS rarely spawns these children. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web application monitoring/health-check scripts that shell out via the app pool
  • Legitimate admin maintenance running cmd/powershell deployment tasks under the IIS identity
  • APM agents or backup jobs invoking net.exe/tasklist from a web context
  • Custom web apps that legitimately call sqlcmd.exe for reporting
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\Monitoring\\","appcmd list"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the child ProcessCommandLine and the requesting URL/IP in the IIS logs (W3CIISLog) for the timeframe; identify the dropped .aspx in the web root. 2) Contain: take the affected app pool/site offline or isolate the server, capture and remove the web shell, and rotate any service-account/MS SQL credentials reachable from the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the server to the campaign IPs and search for staged web-source-code archives (RAR) and SoftEther/VNT binaries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","aspnet_wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","sqlcmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","aspnet_wp.exe")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","sqlcmd.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TinyRCT C2 and downloader beacon to CL-STA-1062 infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the campaign's hardcoded infrastructure: TinyRCT C2 (45.32.113.172), the loader's download server (139.180.134.221), and SoftEther/VNT tunneling infrastructure (202.182.102.5, 45.76.210.43). High-fidelity because these are fixed, corroborated campaign IOCs. Rationale: Direct match on four corroborated campaign IPs (C2 45.32.113.172 and downloader 139.180.134.221 named in the body; SoftEther/VNT infra from the IOC bundle) — fixed infrastructure IOCs are inherently high-fidelity and surface the initiating process for pivoting. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/china-hackers-asian-cni-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researchers or sandbox detonation hosts intentionally connecting to the IOC IPs
  • Shared Vultr hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service (validate against current passive DNS)
  • Security scanners/EDR validation tooling probing the known-bad IPs
  • VPN/proxy infrastructure coincidentally rehosted on the same address block
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-LAB","DETONATE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — confirm whether it is PerfWatson2.exe or a masqueraded VMware/XDR binary; note beacon cadence (~10s GET). 2) Contain: block the four IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to these IPs, look for the AppDomainManager loader artifacts and SoftEther/VNT/Yuze tooling, and review MS SQL/web-root data access for exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172","139.180.134.221","202.182.102.5","45.76.210.43")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.32.113.172","139.180.134.221","202.182.102.5","45.76.210.43")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Masquerading: VMware/XDR/PerfWatson binaries from non-standard paths AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 tooling disguised as trusted VMware or XDR binaries (vmtools.exe, vmwared.exe, XDRAgent.exe, PerfWatson2.exe) executing from paths or with publisher metadata that don't match the legitimate products. Article-specific to the group's masquerading defense-evasion technique. Rationale: Targets the exact masquerade filenames Unit 42 listed (XDRAgent.exe, vmtools.exe, vmwared.exe) plus the TinyRCT payload name PerfWatson2.exe, gated on path/publisher mismatch so legitimate VMware Tools and Visual Studio telemetry are excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools (vmtools.exe) running from a non-default install path after a custom deployment
  • Visual Studio's legitimate PerfWatson2.exe executing from a non-standard developer toolchain path
  • Third-party XDR/EDR product legitimately shipping an XDRAgent.exe binary in the environment
  • Software-distribution staging directories temporarily holding signed VMware binaries
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in ("00e09754526d0fe836ba27e3144ae161b0ecd3774abec5560504a16a67f0087c","f34bd1d485de437fe18360d1e850c3fd64415e49d691e610711d8d232071a0b1","dce5df29bddff5a4ddaea5c4fec14da91f7b69063a6e1c45ed61e5da4fc6c87b","cbfe8de6ffadbb1d396f61e63eb18e8b11c29527c1528641e3223d4c516cf7c3","4e1f8888d020decd09799ec946f1bf677cac6612b24582ddbf4d8ede425d8384","9b481b69cd91b09fa7bae7428f646dd89473a4c03393e43da81fe756cde1c472") or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName == ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the binary's signature, publisher (CompanyName), and SHA256 against the campaign hashes; verify the parent process and folder path. 2) Contain: if unsigned or hash matches, isolate the host, kill and quarantine the binary, and block its C2 (45.32.113.172). 3) Hunt: enumerate SoftEther VPN, VNT, and Yuze SOCKS5 components on the host, review for unexpected VPN/proxy tunnels, and sweep the fleet for the same filename-from-wrong-path pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe","vmwared.exe","XDRAgent.exe","PerfWatson2.exe")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\VMware\" and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "VMware")
| where not(FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe" and FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe","vmwared.exe","XDRAgent.exe","PerfWatson2.exe")
| where not(TargetProcessName endswith "PerfWatson2.exe" and TargetProcessFileCompany has "Microsoft")
| where not(TargetProcessFileCompany has "VMware")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT toolset known-bad SHA256 execution or file write AIInstallation Medium
High-confidence alert matching the six corroborated CL-STA-1062 file hashes (TinyRCT and toolset) across process execution, file writes, and DLL loads. A direct IOC sweep for the campaign's binaries. Rationale: Direct sweep on the six pre-extracted SHA256 IOCs across execution, file-write, and DLL-load telemetry; hash matches are the highest-fidelity signal available and need no behavioural context. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host with the samples staged for analysis
  • Legitimate AV/EDR quarantine store retaining a copy of a detected sample (file-write event on the quarantine path)
  • Security-team retro-hunt importing the samples to a forensic workstation
  • Hash collision is cryptographically negligible — effectively no benign FP outside lab handling
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-LAB","FORENSIC","QUARANTINE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a known malware-analysis/quarantine system; capture the file path, parent process, and first-seen time. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the matching binary, and block 45.32.113.172 / 139.180.134.221. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to lateral-movement infra (202.182.102.5, 45.76.210.43), look for the AppDomainManager loader and web-shell artifacts, and sweep the fleet for all six hashes.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHashes = dynamic(["00e09754526d0fe836ba27e3144ae161b0ecd3774abec5560504a16a67f0087c","f34bd1d485de437fe18360d1e850c3fd64415e49d691e610711d8d232071a0b1","dce5df29bddff5a4ddaea5c4fec14da91f7b69063a6e1c45ed61e5da4fc6c87b","cbfe8de6ffadbb1d396f61e63eb18e8b11c29527c1528641e3223d4c516cf7c3","4e1f8888d020decd09799ec946f1bf677cac6612b24582ddbf4d8ede425d8384","9b481b69cd91b09fa7bae7428f646dd89473a4c03393e43da81fe756cde1c472"]);
