Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Hotel booking phishing via Calendly authentication laundering ('Booking Manager') · [LLM] PNG-masquerading LNK / photo-*.zip dropped to disk (double extension .png.lnk) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LNK-launched PowerShell using BigInt arithmetic to decode a download URL · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CISA Adds Exploited PTC Windchill RCE Flaw to KEV as Web Shell Attacks Continue
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js runtime executing JavaScript implant from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs (TonRAT) · [LLM] TonRAT persistence: Node.js Run key and RunOnce entry into ProgramData · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TonRAT C2 beaconing: node.exe to fixed IPs over non-standard ports · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TonRAT hands-on actions: node.exe spawning forced shutdown or headless browser · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Hotel booking phishing via Calendly authentication laundering ('Booking Manager') AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail abusing Calendly's notification system (display name 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)') to launder SPF/DKIM/DMARC and deliver photo-themed lure links to hotel front-desk mailboxes. Article-specific to the TonRAT hospitality campaign that routes Calendly -> share.google -> Cloudflare .cfd domains. Rationale: Keys on the exact lure display name 'Booking Manager' arriving from authorized calendly.com infrastructure (the 'authentication laundering' trick Microsoft describes); EmailUrlInfo surfaces the share.google/.cfd redirect chain for triage. Sentinel left empty: this tenant's documented schema has no EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/technical-analysis-of-suspicious-emails-targeting-the-hotel-industry/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Calendly booking-confirmation notifications to a real reservations team
  • A hotel chain that genuinely names an internal contact 'Booking Manager' and uses Calendly for scheduling
  • Marketing/partner invites sent through Calendly with a manager display name
  • Internal staff forwarding a real Calendly link inbound from a personal account
Suppression filter
| where UrlDomain !endswith "calendly.com" or isnotempty(UrlDomain)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the EmailUrlInfo URL and follow the redirect class - genuine Calendly links resolve to calendly.com; campaign links chain through share.google to a .cfd/.xyz/.click domain. Check EmailLanguage (Japanese/Danish/Dutch are the campaign's lures). 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine matching messages tenant-wide via NetworkMessageId, and block the resolved final-hop domains at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot any recipient who clicked to UrlClickEvents, then to DeviceFileEvents for photo-*.zip / *.png.lnk drops on their host.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager"
| where SenderFromDomain has "calendly.com" or SenderMailFromDomain has "calendly.com"
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromAddress,
          SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailLanguage,
          DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager"
| where SenderFromDomain has "calendly.com" or SenderMailFromDomain has "calendly.com"
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderDisplayName, SenderFromAddress,
          SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailLanguage,
          DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc
PNG-masquerading LNK / photo-*.zip dropped to disk (double extension .png.lnk) AIDelivery High
Detects the campaign's lure artifacts hitting disk: photo-<numbers>.zip archives and the contained IMG-<numbers>.png.lnk / PHOTO-<numbers>.png.lnk shortcuts that pose as images via a double extension. High fidelity because legitimate software almost never writes a .png.lnk file. Rationale: Uses the article's exact artifact naming - photo-<numbers>.zip and the IMG/PHOTO-<numbers>.png.lnk double extension; a .png.lnk write is intrinsically anomalous, making this near-zero-FP alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/technical-analysis-of-suspicious-emails-targeting-the-hotel-industry/
ATT&CKT1036.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/designer ZIP genuinely prefixed 'photo-' (rare and never produces .png.lnk)
  • Backup or archival tooling repackaging photo libraries into photo-*.zip
  • Security tooling staging the sample itself for analysis on an analyst host
  • User-created shortcut accidentally named with .png before .lnk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .png.lnk's parent write process (browser/explorer/zip tool) and the originating download URL via FileOriginUrl; inspect the LNK target string for a powershell one-liner. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the LNK was executed (check DeviceProcessEvents for a child powershell.exe), and quarantine the file by SHA256. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same SHA256s and for any node.exe running under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs (the implant stage).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".png.lnk"
   or (FileName startswith "photo-" and FileName endswith ".zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".png.lnk"
   or (TargetFileName startswith "photo-" and TargetFileName endswith ".zip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects photo-themed ZIP archives and double-extension .png.lnk shortcuts used by the TonRAT hospitality phishing campaign.

LNK-launched PowerShell using BigInt arithmetic to decode a download URL AIExploitation High
Detects the execution stage where opening the .png.lnk fires PowerShell that uses BigInt arithmetic to decode a hidden download URL and pulls a .ps1 to %TEMP%. Parent is explorer.exe (shortcut double-click) and the command line carries the campaign's BigInt decoder. Rationale: 'BigInt' as a URL-decode primitive in a PowerShell command line spawned by explorer.exe is a distinctive, article-named technique - the combination is far tighter than generic Office/browser->PowerShell rules already in place. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1204.002 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer testing BigInt math in an interactive PowerShell window launched from Explorer
  • Legitimate installer shortcuts that wrap PowerShell with large-integer license checks
  • RMM tooling that uses BigInt for checksum routines
  • Security training labs reproducing the technique
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the BigInt expression to recover the staged URL; check %TEMP% (DeviceFileEvents) for the freshly written .ps1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the powershell process tree, and block the recovered download URL/domain. 3) Hunt: follow the chain forward to a Node.js runtime drop under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs and outbound beacons to the campaign IPs/ports.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "BigInt"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "[bigint]"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has "explorer.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "BigInt" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "[bigint]"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js runtime executing JavaScript implant from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs (TonRAT) AIInstallation High
Detects the TonRAT implant stage: a user-space Node.js v24.13.0 runtime planted under AppData\Local\Nodejs executing a .js file. A legitimate Node binary running from a per-user AppData path (no system-wide install) is the campaign's signature, used to avoid a system-wide Node footprint. Rationale: Pins on the exact persistence/runtime path AppData\Local\Nodejs for node.exe (a signed, legit binary) - the location, not the binary, is the IOC, which is what makes this high-fidelity rather than a generic 'node.exe ran' alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/technical-analysis-of-suspicious-emails-targeting-the-hotel-industry/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using a portable/nvm-style per-user Node install under AppData
  • Electron apps that bundle node.exe (but typically under their own app folder, not AppData\Local\Nodejs)
  • VS Code / build tooling spawning a user-scoped Node
  • Legitimate fnm/volta version managers placing node in AppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","volta.exe","fnm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm there is no sanctioned per-user Node deployment for this user/host; inspect the .js argument and node.exe ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion (campaign uses 24.13.0) plus the parent (should trace to the staged .ps1). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the node.exe tree; remove the runtime and .js under AppData\Local\Nodejs. 3) Hunt: pull both persistence paths - the RunOnce entry into ProgramData and the Node.js Run key - and check DeviceNetworkEvents for beacons to the campaign IPs/ports.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TonRAT C2 beaconing: node.exe to fixed IPs over non-standard ports AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the implant's post-compromise C2: the AppData\Local\Nodejs node.exe beaconing to the campaign's hard-coded IPs and non-standard ports (8443, 8445, 8453, 5555, 56001-56003). TonRAT resolves additional C2 via the TON blockchain API but falls back to these fixed endpoints. Rationale: Combines the four corroborated C2 IPs with the campaign's specific non-standard port set, scoped to the AppData node.exe - both halves are article IOCs, giving a low-FP alerting rule even though 8443 alone would be noisy (so 8443 is excluded from the process-less Sentinel port path). Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/technical-analysis-of-suspicious-emails-targeting-the-hotel-industry/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001 T1102.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal node app connecting to an 8443 HTTPS-alt service (mitigated by the AppData path + IP IOCs)
  • Network/management appliances using 5555 internally
  • Vulnerability scanners probing the campaign ports across the estate
  • A reused/recycled cloud IP that previously hosted C2 now serving benign content
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating node.exe lives under AppData\Local\Nodejs and correlate the connection time to the implant launch; capture the destination IP/port and any RemoteUrl. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the four C2 IPs and the rare ports (8445/8453/5555/56001-56003) at the firewall, and capture memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: query DNS/proxy for the campaign .cfd/.xyz/.click domains and any toncenter/TON blockchain API lookups from node.exe to find sibling infected reception hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
| where RemoteIP in ("178.16.54.27","95.217.97.121","193.202.84.32","178.16.55.179")
   or RemotePort in (8443, 8445, 8453, 5555, 56001, 56002, 56003)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("178.16.54.27","95.217.97.121","193.202.84.32","178.16.55.179")
   or DstPortNumber in (8445, 8453, 5555, 56001, 56002, 56003)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DstHostname, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TonRAT persistence: Node.js Run key and RunOnce entry into ProgramData AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's dual persistence: a Run key launching the AppData Node.js implant and a RunOnce entry pointing into ProgramData. Microsoft stresses both must be removed - pulling one leaves the other alive - so each registry write is worth alerting on. Rationale: Targets both persistence paths Microsoft calls out (AppData Node.js Run key + ProgramData RunOnce); the value-data anchors (\AppData\Local\Nodejs, \ProgramData\) make it specific to this implant rather than generic Run-key noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate per-user Node app (Slack/Teams-style Electron helper) registering a Run key referencing node.exe
  • Sanctioned software staged in ProgramData adding a RunOnce updater
  • Endpoint management tooling writing autostart entries during deployment
  • Developer auto-launch scripts pointing at a personal Node build
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","Code.exe") and RegistryValueData !has "Microsoft\\Edge"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read both RegistryValueData values and confirm whether they reference AppData\Local\Nodejs and/or a ProgramData binary; identify the writing process. 2) Contain: remove BOTH the Run key and the RunOnce entry (removing one leaves the other), then delete the referenced runtime/.js and ProgramData payload. 3) Hunt: confirm the node.exe runtime under AppData and any C2 beacons; sweep other reception/reservations hosts for the same Run/RunOnce value-data pattern.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" or RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce"
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
   or RegistryValueData has "node.exe"
   or RegistryValueData has @"\ProgramData\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" or RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce"
| where RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
   or RegistryValueData has "node.exe"
   or RegistryValueData has @"\ProgramData\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue,
          RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TonRAT hands-on actions: node.exe spawning forced shutdown or headless browser AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-compromise operator actions where the AppData Node.js implant spawns a forced shutdown (cmd /c shutdown -s -t 0) or launches a headless browser (--headless --no-sandbox). Parent process is node.exe, which distinguishes it from routine admin shutdowns or normal browser launches. Rationale: node.exe as the parent of either 'shutdown -s -t 0' or a '--headless --no-sandbox' browser launch are the two operator actions Microsoft observed; the node.exe parentage (plus AppData path) is what keeps a routine shutdown or Chrome launch from firing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/
ATT&CKT1529 T1059.007 T1614
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate node automation/test harness driving Chrome/Edge headless with --no-sandbox in CI on a build host
  • An IT script using node to schedule maintenance reboots
  • Puppeteer/Playwright-based monitoring agents on a kiosk
  • A node-based RMM module issuing a controlled restart
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm node.exe runs from AppData\Local\Nodejs (vs a sanctioned dev/CI Node) and read the full child command line - a forced shutdown -s -t 0 is destructive/anti-forensic intent. 2) Contain: isolate the host before the shutdown completes if caught live, kill the node tree, and snapshot for IR. 3) Hunt: correlate with the implant's ip-api.com geolocation lookups and C2 beacons, and check whether other front-office hosts show the same node.exe-spawned shutdown/headless pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "shutdown" and ProcessCommandLine has "-s" and ProcessCommandLine has "-t")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--headless" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-sandbox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shutdown" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-s" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-t")
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--headless" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-sandbox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TonRAT Post-Compromise - node.exe Spawns Forced Shutdown or Headless Browser
id: b9d3e6a4-7c18-4f52-8a93-2e5c0b7d1f46

description: AppData-resident node.exe launching a forced shutdown or a headless browser, matching TonRAT operator actions.

  selection_headless:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" ((Processes.process="*shutdown*" AND Processes.process="*-s*" AND Processes.process="*-t*") OR (Processes.process="*--headless*" AND Processes.process="*--no-sandbox*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" ((Processes.process="*shutdown*" AND Processes.process="*-s*" AND Processes.process="*-t*") OR (Processes.process="*--headless*" AND Processes.process="*--no-sandbox*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\mshta.exe'

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'

      cross-shell escaping
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

tags:

logsource:

    product: windows
detection:

            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

New DirtyClone Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root via Cloned Packets

The Hacker News
2026-06-26 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

DirtyClone is a new Linux kernel privilege escalation in the DirtyFrag family.&nbsp;JFrog Security Research published a working exploit walkthrough&nbsp;for the flaw on June 25, the first public demonstration for this variant. Tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-43503&nbsp;(CVSS 8.8), it lets a local user corrupt file-backed memory through a cloned network packet and gain root. The patch landed in

Unprivileged user+network namespace creation (DirtyClone CAP_NET_ADMIN path) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a non-root user creating a combined user+network namespace via `unshare --user --net` (or `--map-root-user`), the prerequisite that grants CAP_NET_ADMIN so the local user can configure the loopback IPsec tunnel DirtyClone (CVE-2026-43503) abuses. Article-specific because DirtyClone's only viable path on default Debian/Fedora is namespace-granted CAP_NET_ADMIN. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated precondition: 'unprivileged user namespaces are enabled by default, so a local user can obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN inside a new namespace.' `unshare --user --net` by a non-root user is the manual form of that path. Cross-checked JFrog and Ubuntu advisories which confirm namespace-granted CAP_NET_ADMIN as the default exploit gate. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/ • https://ubuntu.com/blog/dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://www.wiz.io/blog/fragnesia-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-via-esp-in-tcp
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rootless container engines (podman/buildah/crun) creating user+net namespaces for normal containers
  • Bubblewrap (bwrap) sandboxes from Flatpak/Steam apps
  • Chromium/Chrome renderer sandbox using unshare
  • systemd-nspawn / unprivileged LXC test containers
  • CI runners executing rootless container builds
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","buildah","conmon","runc","crun","bwrap","containerd-shim","chrome","chrome_sandbox","steam","flatpak","systemd-nspawn")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the unshare event — confirm the parent is NOT a known container runtime (podman/runc/bwrap) and that the same user/host shows a subsequent `ip xfrm` on loopback (UC pivot). 2) Contain: if no legitimate container context, suspend the user's sessions on that host and snapshot it; reboot only after evidence capture (reboot restores the in-memory-modified binary and destroys the trail). 3) Hunt: search the host for `ip xfrm state/policy add` on 127.0.0.1/::1, esp4/esp6/rxrpc module loads, and any unexpected root shell or su/sudo success in the minutes following the namespace creation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U","--map-root-user")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
| where AccountName != "root" and isnotempty(AccountName)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","buildah","conmon","runc","crun","bwrap","chrome","chrome_sandbox","flatpak")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "unshare"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U","--map-root-user")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
| where ActorUsername != "root" and isnotempty(ActorUsername)
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("podman","buildah","runc","crun","bwrap","chrome","flatpak"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Loopback IPsec/XFRM tunnel configured by local process (DirtyClone write primitive) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts configuration of an IPsec XFRM state/policy bound to loopback (127.0.0.1 / ::1) — the channel DirtyClone forces a cloned, file-backed packet through so esp_input() decryption overwrites /usr/bin/su's login checks in the shared page cache. Loopback IPsec is almost never legitimate, making this the sharpest article-specific signal. Rationale: Uses the article's core mechanic verbatim: the attacker 'configures the loopback IPsec tunnel' and the cloned packet's 'decryption step overwrites the binary's login checks.' XFRM state/policy on 127.0.0.1/::1 is the highest-fidelity, lowest-FP indicator. JFrog and Wiz writeups confirm esp_input()/XFRM as the in-place crypto-transform write vector. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/dirty-frag-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-via-esp-and-rxrpc • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/copy-fail-dirtyfrag-linux-page-bugs-in-the-wild
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually testing/troubleshooting IPsec config against loopback
  • CI/integration tests that exercise the xfrm stack on 127.0.0.1
  • Network plugin (Cilium/Calico WireGuard-fallback) misconfigured to use loopback endpoints
  • strongSwan/libreswan QA harnesses keying loopback SAs
  • Security researchers reproducing DirtyFrag-class PoCs in a lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("charon","starter","ipsec","swanctl","strongswan","libreswan","cilium-agent","calico-node")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full command line — legitimate IPsec terminates on a routable interface, not 127.0.0.1/::1; confirm the invoking user and whether a user+net namespace was created seconds earlier (UC1 pivot). 2) Contain: isolate the host from orchestration (cordon the node if Kubernetes), preserve memory, and force re-auth for any account that ran su/sudo on it — the in-memory su patch hands root to the next caller. 3) Hunt: check for esp4/esp6/rxrpc autoload, unexpected uid 0 processes spawned post-event, and replicate across the cluster since page cache is host-shared and affects every process on the machine.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("ip","setkey")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" or FileName =~ "setkey")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("state add","policy add"," add ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("ip","setkey")
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" or TargetProcessName has "setkey")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("state add","policy add"," add ")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName

Namespace creation followed by loopback IPsec setup (DirtyClone exploit chain) AIExploitation High
Correlates UC1 and UC2 on the same host: a non-root user creates a user+network namespace and, within minutes, configures an IPsec XFRM tunnel on loopback. The two-step temporal chain is the full DirtyClone (CVE-2026-43503) precondition and is far higher fidelity than either step alone. Rationale: Joins the two article-stated steps (namespace-granted CAP_NET_ADMIN, then loopback IPsec tunnel) within a 10-minute window on one host — the complete DirtyClone setup sequence. Temporal correlation removes the residual FP from rootless-container namespace noise and admin IPsec testing seen individually. Sigma/Datadog left empty: cross-event temporal join is not expressible as a single-event-shape rule. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/ • https://ubuntu.com/blog/dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A rootless container runtime that both creates namespaces and programs xfrm for in-cluster encryption on the same node within 10 minutes (rare)
  • Automated IPsec lab/CI that namespaces a test then keys loopback SAs
  • Admin reproducing the DirtyClone PoC for validation
  • Security scanner exploit-check modules running both steps
Response runbook
1) Triage: this chain is high-confidence malicious on a production multi-tenant/CI/K8s host — confirm the user is unprivileged and not a container-runtime service account, and capture both command lines. 2) Contain: immediately isolate/cordon the host, capture volatile memory, and treat root on that machine as compromised — rotate credentials and any secrets cached on it before rebooting (reboot erases the in-memory binary tampering). 3) Hunt: sweep the rest of the cluster/tenant for the same two-step pattern, check kernel version against the CVE-2026-43503 patch (UC4), and review su/sudo/auth logs for anomalous root grants post-event.
let win = 10m;
let ns = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "unshare"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
    | project NsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, NsUser = AccountName, NsCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("ip","setkey")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project IpTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, IpUser = AccountName, IpCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| join kind=inner ns on DeviceId
| where IpTime between (NsTime .. NsTime + win)
| project DeviceName, NsUser, IpUser, NsTime, IpTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', IpTime, NsTime), NsCmd, IpCmd
| order by IpTime desc
let win = 10m;
let ns = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName has "unshare"
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
    | project NsTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, NsUser = ActorUsername, NsCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("ip","setkey")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project IpTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, IpUser = ActorUsername, IpCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| join kind=inner ns on DvcHostname
| where IpTime between (NsTime .. NsTime + win)
| project DvcHostname, NsUser, IpUser, NsTime, IpTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', IpTime, NsTime), NsCmd, IpCmd
| order by IpTime desc

Hosts exposed to DirtyFrag-class kernel LPE (CVE-2026-43503 and siblings) AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt: enumerate Linux hosts whose kernel is still vulnerable to DirtyClone/DirtyFrag-class flaws (CVE-2026-43503 and the related CVE-2026-43284/43500/46300/31431), i.e. missing the v7.1-rc5 / commit 48f6a5356a33 backport. Prioritises multi-tenant servers, CI runners and container/K8s hosts where untrusted users can create namespaces. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs and patch landmark from the article (fix in v7.1-rc5, commit 48f6a5356a33) plus the corroborated DirtyFrag-class siblings to scope the still-vulnerable fleet. Pure inventory hunt — no behavioural Splunk/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon form, so those are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against Red Hat RHSB-2026-003 and Ubuntu advisory which enumerate the same CVE cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-003 • https://ubuntu.com/blog/dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/

Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM scan where the kernel was patched but the device hasn't re-reported
  • Live-patched kernels (kpatch/livepatch) not reflected in version string
  • Containers double-counted against the host kernel they share
  • EOL/isolated appliances flagged but not reachable by untrusted users
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by exposure — multi-tenant, CI runner, container/K8s nodes with unprivileged-userns enabled go first; verify the running kernel actually lacks commit 48f6a5356a33 (not just a stale scan). 2) Contain: where patching can't happen immediately, apply the article's stopgaps — set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 and/or blacklist esp4/esp6/rxrpc — then schedule the kernel update from stable/LTS. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, run UC2/UC3 retroactively over 30 days to confirm the loopback-IPsec primitive was never exercised before patching.

Miasma/Shai-Hulud binding.gyp install-time exec spawning Bun stealer AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma execution chain where a trojanized npm package's binding.gyp triggers node-gyp during install, launching a JS loader that downloads the legitimate Bun runtime and runs the decrypted stealer (written to /tmp/p<random>.js) under Bun instead of Node. Article-specific because it pairs the binding.gyp parent context with a node/npm/node-gyp -> bun process transition. Rationale: Anchors on the article's documented chain (binding.gyp -> node-gyp -> JS loader -> Bun runtime -> /tmp/p<random>.js), corroborated by JFrog/safedep/Endor; node-spawning-bun during dependency resolution is rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native npm modules that genuinely require node-gyp/binding.gyp compilation during install (e.g. bcrypt, sharp, node-sass)
  • Developers intentionally using the Bun runtime as a Node replacement in build scripts
  • CI runners that pre-warm Bun for legitimate test pipelines
  • Monorepo postinstall hooks that shell out to bun for tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bcrypt","node-sass","sharp","sqlite3") and ProcessCommandLine !matches regex @"(?i)/tmp/p[a-z0-9]+\.js")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the bun.exe launch — confirm the parent is node/node-gyp during an npm install and inspect the script path (/tmp/p<random>.js is malicious). Capture SHA1 and compare to 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke any npm/GitHub PATs and OIDC tokens used on it, and quarantine the offending node_modules tree. 3) Hunt: search the same host/org for the dead-drop markers (UC5), 'Run Copilot' workflow drops (UC3), and outbound GitHub beaconing (UC4).

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","node-gyp.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","sh","bash","cmd.exe"))
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("binding.gyp","node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp build") and FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun","node.exe","node"))
    or (FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/tmp/p[a-z0-9]+\.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized LeoPlatform/RStreams npm package landing via binding.gyp drop AIDelivery High
Detects the supply-chain landing of the compromised czirker-maintained Leo/RStreams packages by flagging creation of a binding.gyp file inside a node_modules subtree of one of the named malicious packages. The Miasma wave uniquely ships binding.gyp (no package.json lifecycle hook), so a binding.gyp under these specific package dirs is a direct supply-chain compromise indicator. Rationale: Uses the exact compromised package names from the article (leo-*, rstreams-*, serverless-leo, prism-silq, solo-nav, hexo-*) combined with the Miasma-unique binding.gyp drop mechanism, corroborated by safedep/Sonatype as the czirker wave's signature. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/miasma-returns-leo-platform-compromise-in-npm

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely benign future release of one of these packages that legitimately needs native compilation (verify version against the published malicious list)
  • Internal mirror/proxy caching the package directory during forensic preservation
  • Security researcher detonating a sample in a sandbox that shares telemetry
  • Package name collision where an unrelated internal package reuses a 'leo-' prefix
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version matches the published malicious set (e.g. leo-sdk 6.0.19, leo-aws 2.0.4, rstreams-metrics 2.0.2); inspect the binding.gyp body for the loader stub. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, remove the package, purge npm cache, and rotate every credential reachable from that workstation/CI (npm tokens, GitHub PATs/OIDC, AWS keys). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (bun execution) on the same host and check your internal registry/lockfiles org-wide for the pinned malicious versions.

Miasma 'Run Copilot' GitHub Actions workflow dropped by node/bun AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Miasma collection stage where the worm writes a malicious workflow (observed as 'Run Copilot') into a repo's .github/workflows directory to scrape CI runner memory for secrets. Differentiator is that the workflow YAML is created/modified by node/bun/npm (the malware) rather than an editor or git, which is anomalous for workflow definitions. Rationale: Targets the article's 'Run Copilot' CI-secret-scraping workflow drop; keying on workflow YAML written by node/bun (not git/editor) is the article-specific anomaly since legitimate workflow edits come from developers or VCS tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1119 T1552.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workflow scaffolding tools (e.g. 'npx', plopjs, hygen) that legitimately generate workflow YAML via node
  • Repo bootstrap scripts that template .github/workflows on project init
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation run locally that rewrites workflow files
  • IaC/codegen pipelines that emit GitHub Actions YAML as build output
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("plop","hygen","yeoman","yo ","create-react-app","renovate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow YAML and check for a 'Run Copilot' job, runner-memory/secret dumping, or steps that read $GITHUB_TOKEN/secrets context; correlate the writing process to a Miasma npm install. 2) Contain: remove the workflow file, block the push if not yet committed, and rotate all repo/org Actions secrets and OIDC trust. 3) Hunt: search the org for any pushed 'Run Copilot' workflow and for new public repos described 'Alright Lets See If This Works' (exfil sink).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.github\workflows\", "/.github/workflows/")
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","npm.exe","npm-cli.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.github\workflows\", "/.github/workflows/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".yml" or TargetFileName endswith ".yaml"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma GitHub dead-drop C2 hourly beaconing from node/bun AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma/Hades command-and-control pattern of hourly polling of GitHub (commit search for 'firedalazer'/'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom' markers) by a node or bun process. Surfaces non-interactive, regularly-cadenced GitHub API traffic from the runtime that executed the stealer — distinct from a developer's interactive git usage. Rationale: Implements the article's hourly GitHub dead-drop C2 (poll for 'firedalazer' to pull Hades) by counting per-host distinct hour-buckets of GitHub traffic from node/bun — corroborated by OX Security/Endor Labs; process attribution to the runtime separates worm beaconing from interactive git. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dependency tooling (npm/renovate/dependabot mirror sync) that legitimately polls GitHub on a schedule from node
  • CI agents fetching releases/tags from GitHub hourly
  • A developer running a long-lived watch/build process that periodically hits the GitHub API
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs bundled in node apps that report to GitHub Pages or raw.githubusercontent.com
Suppression filter
| where SampleCmd !has_any ("renovate","dependabot","npm install","npm ci","yarn","pnpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the node/bun command line and parent chain — confirm it is the Miasma stealer (UC1) and not a known package manager; inspect the actual GitHub API paths for /search/commits queries. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block egress to GitHub from that process, and revoke GitHub PAT/OIDC tokens it could read. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the dead-drop marker strings (UC5) and any retrieved Hades index.js written to temp.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com","codeload.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), HourBuckets = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| where HourBuckets >= 6   // regular polling across >=6 distinct hours = beaconing cadence (worm polls hourly for 'firedalazer')
| order by HourBuckets desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("api.github.com","github.com","codeload.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), HourBuckets = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where HourBuckets >= 6   // hourly GitHub dead-drop poll cadence
| order by HourBuckets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\bun.exe OR */node OR */bun) @DestinationHostname:(*github.com OR *githubusercontent.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(api\.github\.com|codeload\.github\.com|raw\.githubusercontent\.com|^github\.com)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|bun)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| count > 6
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (Network_Resolution.query="api.github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="codeload.github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="raw.githubusercontent.com") by Network_Resolution.src Network_Resolution.query _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Resolution)`
| stats dc(_time) as hour_buckets sum(count) as total min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src query
| where hour_buckets >= 6
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - hour_buckets
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (Network_Resolution.query="api.github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="codeload.github.com" OR Network_Resolution.query="raw.githubusercontent.com") by Network_Resolution.src Network_Resolution.query _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Resolution)`
| stats dc(_time) as hour_buckets sum(count) as total min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src query
| where hour_buckets >= 6
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - hour_buckets
Shai-Hulud/Miasma unique dead-drop marker strings & payload hash on endpoint AICommand & Control High
High-fidelity catch-all for the campaign's rotating but unique relay markers and the known stealer hash. Matches 'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom', 'firedalazer', the exfil repo description 'Alright Lets See If This Works', the legacy 'IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner' string, or SHA1 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5 appearing in process command lines / script content. Rationale: Matches the article's verbatim, campaign-unique strings (RevokeAndItGoesKaboom, firedalazer, the 'Alright Lets See If This Works' exfil-repo description, legacy nuke-token marker) plus the pre-extracted stealer SHA1 — these are near-zero-FP IOCs confirmed by StepSecurity and JFrog. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/
ATT&CKT1027.013 T1102.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst pasting these IOC strings into a terminal/script during research
  • An EDR/AV signature update or YARA rule file containing the marker strings being read on disk
  • Blog/article text containing the strings cached locally and opened by a process
  • A SOAR playbook that references the marker strings in its automation code
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","notepad++.exe","grep","rg.exe","findstr.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("yara","sigma","ioc","threat-intel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match is live malware execution (not analyst research or an IOC list) by checking the host, process lineage, and whether the SHA1 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5 is present. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, revoke all GitHub PAT/OIDC tokens, npm publish tokens, AWS keys and Vault creds reachable from it, and search GitHub for repos/commits carrying these markers under your org. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1/UC2 (bun exec + malicious package install) on the same host and across the org's CI fleet, and audit recent package publishes from the affected identities.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","firedalazer","Alright Lets See If This Works","IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner")
        or SHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
        or InitiatingProcessSHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","firedalazer","Alright Lets See If This Works","IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner")
    or SHA1 =~ "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
