File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal drop into Startup folder (Turla STOCKSTAY delivery) AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific CVE-2025-8088 exploitation pattern GTIG observed delivering STOCKSTAY: a vulnerable WinRAR/UnRAR extracting an archive that uses an Alternate Data Stream + directory-traversal path to write an executable payload (.lnk/.exe/.dll/.hta) into the per-user Windows Startup folder for auto-execution at next logon. Archive tools should never write into Startup. Rationale: Built on GTIG's confirmed CVE-2025-8088 signature (archive tool + ADS traversal writing an executable into per-user Startup) which multiple second sources (ESET, SOCPrime, ThreatLocker) corroborate as the consistent persistence mechanism for STOCKSTAY/RomCom/Sandworm deliveries; the archive-process + Startup-path + executable-extension triple is high-fidelity because legitimate archive extraction never targets Startup. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/update-winrar-tools-now-romcom-and-others-exploiting-zero-day-vulnerability/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable apps extracted directly into a user profile that legitimately ship a Startup shortcut (rare)
  • Software-deployment tooling that wraps installers in self-extracting RAR and adds a Startup launcher
  • Admin manually extracting a utility into Startup for a kiosk/shared machine
  • Backup/sync agents re-materialising a previously-existing Startup .lnk via an archive extraction
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's SHA256 and FolderPath; confirm the parent archive tool and the source .rar (check Downloads/mail-attachment dirs). Detonate or hash-lookup the dropped payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Startup artifact, and quarantine the originating RAR; block the file hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: confirm WinRAR version <7.13 across the fleet via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory; sweep for the same SHA256 / Startup-folder writes on other endpoints and for follow-on STOCKSTAY components (websocket-sharp.dll, masqueraded PDF/calculator binaries).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","wzzip.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".scr"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","wzzip.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("lnk","exe","dll","hta","cmd","bat","js","vbs","scr")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Payload Written to Startup Folder
id: 7c2e1d44-9f3b-4a0e-bf21-3a9d5e8c1b40
description: Archive utility (WinRAR/UnRAR) writing an executable file into the Windows Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal abuse used to deliver Turla STOCKSTAY.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\7zfm.exe'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.lnk'
      - '.exe'
      - '.dll'
      - '.hta'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.bat'
      - '.js'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.scr'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\unrar.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe OR *\\7zfm.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\Start?Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\* OR *\\start?menu\\programs\\startup\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|unrar|rar|7zfm)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\Start Menu\\\\Programs\\\\Startup\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| TargetFileName=/\.(lnk|exe|dll|hta|cmd|bat|js|vbs|scr)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.scr") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.scr") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Malicious .RDP email attachment opened — mstsc launched from mail/download dir (Turla initial access) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the early-2025 STOCKSTAY initial-access vector GTIG documented: a phishing email with a malicious .rdp attachment that, when opened, runs mstsc.exe to connect the victim to actor-controlled RDP infrastructure (a beachhead for deploying STOCKSTAY). Detects mstsc.exe invoked against a .rdp file located in a mail-attachment, download, or temp directory. Rationale: Uses GTIG's documented STOCKSTAY beachhead (phishing email carrying a malicious .rdp attachment that auto-establishes a connection to actor infra); requiring mstsc.exe + a .rdp path inside a mail/download/temp directory excludes routine internal RDP (which references saved .rdp in profile/Documents or no file at all), making attachment-borne .rdp launches high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT support emailing a one-off .rdp jump-host file that a user saves to Downloads and double-clicks
  • User downloading a .rdp connection profile from an internal SharePoint/portal into Downloads
  • MSP remote-support tooling that stages an .rdp file in %TEMP% before launch
  • Power user keeping ad-hoc .rdp files in their Downloads folder for convenience
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Documents\", @"\Program Files\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"Content.Outlook")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the .rdp file path and read its 'full address:s:' / 'gatewayhostname' targets; resolve whether the destination is external/actor infrastructure vs a known internal jump host. Pull the originating email (sender, subject, attachment hash). 2) Contain: block the RDP destination IP/host at the firewall, quarantine the source email tenant-wide, and isolate the host if the connection succeeded outbound. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for mstsc.exe outbound to Public IPs from this and other hosts; sweep for follow-on STOCKSTAY artifacts (websocket-sharp.dll, Startup-folder drops, masqueraded PDF/calculator .NET binaries).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".rdp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Content.Outlook\", @"\INetCache\", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Olk\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe","winrar.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mstsc.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".rdp"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\Content.Outlook\", @"\INetCache\", @"\Olk\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: Remote Desktop Client Launched From Malicious .RDP Attachment

STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER: mshta from RAR archive reaching internet to pull ZIP from compromised WordPress AIExploitation High
Hunts the RAR-delivered HTA execution chain GTIG attributed to STOCKSTAY: a .rar containing an HTA script runs mshta.exe (the STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER downloader variant), which then retrieves a ZIP of the main STOCKSTAY components from a compromised WordPress site. Pivots on mshta.exe spawned by an archive utility and/or making an outbound connection to a public host. Rationale: Grounded in GTIG's described chain (RAR-with-HTA -> mshta executes STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER -> downloads ZIP from a compromised WordPress host); mshta.exe parented by an archive extractor is an inherently abnormal LOLBin lineage, and the Defender variant adds the public-IP egress that captures the WordPress ZIP pull. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon use the process-tree shape since those schemas lack the parent-on-network field (noted divergence). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business app shipped as a RAR self-extractor that launches an .hta installer
  • Help-desk packaging an HTA utility inside a RAR for distribution
  • Explorer-launched .hta double-clicked by a developer testing legacy HTA tooling
  • Software updater that extracts and runs an HTA configuration wizard
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Windows\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture mshta's command line and the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP it contacted; determine the source .rar and whether a .zip was written to disk afterward. 2) Contain: block the download URL/host (likely a compromised WordPress site), isolate the host, and quarantine the originating RAR/HTA. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by mshta and any child processes; sweep for the downloaded ZIP and extracted STOCKSTAY components (STOCKBROKER/STOCKTRADER, websocket-sharp.dll) and for Startup-folder persistence on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","explorer.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

STOCKSTAY websocket-sharp tunneler (STOCKBROKER) loaded by masqueraded .NET process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the STOCKSTAY.STOCKBROKER tunneler component, which establishes the secure-WebSocket C2 using the open-source websocket-sharp library. Surfaces the websocket-sharp.dll being loaded/dropped by a user-writable, masquerading binary (PDF viewer / calculator / stock-market viewer names) — the disguise GTIG says STOCKSTAY adopts. Rationale: Pivots on the named open-source library GTIG explicitly states STOCKSTAY.STOCKBROKER uses (websocket-sharp) combined with STOCKSTAY's documented masquerade (PDF viewer / calculator / stock viewer) and a user-writable load/drop path; websocket-sharp is uncommon in enterprise software, so its presence under AppData/Temp/Public is a strong STOCKSTAY tunneler indicator. Sentinel left empty: no image-load/DLL-load table is available in this tenant's schema. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party .NET application bundling websocket-sharp.dll and installed under AppData (e.g. some chat/streaming clients)
  • Developer/test machines with .NET projects that reference websocket-sharp in a build/temp output folder
  • Portable open-source tools shipping websocket-sharp from a Public or ProgramData directory
  • Game launchers or IoT companion apps using websocket-sharp for local control channels
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the loading/dropping process (name, path, SHA256, signer) and check whether it is unsigned and masquerading as a PDF/calculator/stock tool; pull its outbound connections for wss/WebSocket traffic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and block the C2 endpoint; quarantine the binary and websocket-sharp.dll. 3) Hunt: correlate to a preceding WinRAR-Startup drop, .rdp attachment, or mshta download; sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for the sibling STOCKSTAY components (STOCKMARKET orchestrator, STOCKTRADER) and WM_COPYDATA/IPC-based multi-process clusters.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "websocket-sharp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pdf","calc","stock","viewer","reader")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "websocket-sharp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pdf","calc","stock","viewer","reader")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Photo ZIP campaign targeting hospitality industry delivers Node.js implant for persistent access

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-25 15 use cases 22 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified an active multi-stage intrusion campaign targeting hospitality organizations in Europe and Asia. The campaign uses photo-themed ZIP archives and fake image shortcut files to deliver a persistent Node.js implant and evade detection. The post Photo ZIP campaign targeting hospitality industry delivers Node.js implant for persistent access appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js implant C2 beacon to safedocphoto/recallnine/kentjerk/photodoc-secure .info domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Calendly authentication-laundering phish: 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' lure to hospitality staff AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail whose sender display name is the campaign's exact 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' string, relayed through Calendly notification infrastructure to launder SPF/DKIM/DMARC before landing on a Cloudflare-gated .cfd download page. Article-specific because the display name, relay domain and .cfd download destination are all named IOCs. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim sender display name 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' plus the Calendly relay domain and .cfd download page — high-fidelity because legitimate hotels rarely receive booking notices spoofing that exact display name via Calendly's notification system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Calendly booking notifications forwarded into shared reception mailboxes
  • Legitimate marketing or scheduling tools that set a 'via Calendly' display name
  • Internal staff testing a real Calendly integration
  • Security awareness phishing simulations reusing hospitality lures
Suppression filter
| where SenderMailFromAddress !endswith "@calendly.com" or isnotempty(UrlDomain) and UrlDomain endswith ".cfd"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SenderMailFromAddress vs SenderDisplayName mismatch and pull the EmailUrlInfo URL chain — flag any redirect ending on a *.cfd or freshly-registered domain. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, block the .cfd domain at the proxy, and warn the recipient reception accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot any clicking user to DeviceFileEvents for photo-<digits>.zip downloads and to the Node.js implant detections (UC3/UC6) on their device within the next 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager (via Calendly)"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager (via Calendly)"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Photo ZIP campaign delivery artifacts: IMG-/PHOTO-*.png.lnk and photo-<digits>.zip AIDelivery High
Hunts on-disk creation of the campaign's fake-image shortcuts (IMG-<digits>.png.lnk and PHOTO-<digits>.png.lnk) and the photo-<digits>.zip source archives dropped via browser download. Article-specific because both naming patterns and the 1,989-2,079 byte LNK size are named delivery IOCs. Rationale: Uses the article's two exact filename grammars (IMG-/PHOTO-<digits>.png.lnk, photo-<digits>.zip) plus the documented 1,989-2,079 byte LNK size band — a double-extension .png.lnk written by a browser is almost never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ZIPs literally named photo-<digits>.zip from a real photo-sharing workflow
  • Backup/sync tools renaming .lnk shortcuts in Downloads
  • Forensic/IR tooling extracting samples to disk during analysis
  • User-created shortcuts that coincidentally match (rare — double extension .png.lnk is the discriminator)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("7zfm.exe","winrar.exe") and FileName endswith ".zip")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .lnk has a double extension and was written by a browser (InitiatingProcessFileName in chrome/msedge/firefox) and that a sibling photo-<digits>.zip exists in Downloads. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the LNK has executed (correlate to powershell.exe child), and quarantine the ZIP+LNK. 3) Hunt: search the same device and account for the Node.js implant path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs\*.js (UC3) and Add-MpPreference exclusions (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(IMG|PHOTO)-\d+\.png\.lnk$" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^photo-\d+\.zip$"
| extend SuspectLnkSize = (FileName endswith ".lnk" and FileSize between (1989 .. 2079))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SuspectLnkSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(IMG|PHOTO)-\d+\.png\.lnk$" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^photo-\d+\.zip$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Node.js implant: node.exe running random .js from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs with a domain argument AIInstallation High
Hunts node.exe executing a randomly-named .js script out of %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs — the campaign's resident implant launch pattern, typically followed by a C2 domain argument. Article-specific because the per-user Nodejs script path and script-plus-domain invocation are named in the captured command lines. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim implant path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs\<random>.js from the captured node.exe command lines; legitimate Node apps install under Program Files or project dirs, not a randomly-named script in the user's local AppData Nodejs folder. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer-installed Node tooling that happens to cache scripts under AppData\Local
  • Electron-app helper processes invoking node from a local AppData path
  • nvm/fnm Node version managers running scripts from user AppData
  • Legitimate npm global packages launched via node from a user directory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code.exe","electron.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","nvm","fnm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine — confirm a randomly-named .js plus a trailing domain argument (e.g. safedocphoto.info), and capture the node.exe SHA256 and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill the node.exe tree, and remove the %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs script and its Run-key persistence. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for that node.exe reaching .info domains on non-standard ports (UC6) and to Add-MpPreference exclusions (UC5) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Local\Nodejs\"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js implant persistence: PowerShell detached relauncher (process.execPath + unref) AIInstallation High
Hunts the campaign's persistence relauncher — a powershell.exe one-liner that spawns process.execPath via child_process with {detached:true} and .unref() to keep the Node.js implant resident and hidden across reboots. Article-specific because the exact JS relauncher string fragments are in the captured PowerShell command line. Rationale: Uses three co-occurring literal tokens from the captured relauncher (process.execPath, child_process, unref) inside a powershell.exe command line — this JS-in-PowerShell relaunch shape is essentially unique to the implant and not produced by normal PowerShell usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based dev tool wrapping a relaunch in PowerShell during install (rare)
  • CI/build agents that re-spawn node detached from a PowerShell wrapper
  • Electron auto-update routines that relaunch the host process
  • Legitimate admin scripts copy-pasting Node child_process snippets for testing
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code.exe","electron.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "node_modules")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell command and the parent process; confirm it references a %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs script. 2) Contain: kill the powershell/node tree, remove the dropped script, and delete the associated Run-key value pointing at node.exe. 3) Hunt: enumerate HKCU/HKLM Run keys referencing node.exe across the fleet and correlate with the implant execution (UC3) and C2 beaconing (UC6).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "process.execPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "unref"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "child_process"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "powershell.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "process.execPath"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "unref"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "child_process"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender process-exclusion for %TEMP% executable via Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess AIInstallation High
Hunts the campaign's defense-evasion step: powershell.exe invoking Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess pointing at a randomly-named EXE under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp, carving out the dropped PE payloads from Defender. Article-specific because the exact Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess + %TEMP% EXE pattern is in the captured command lines. Rationale: Combines the literal Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess flag with a %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp path (verbatim @-string, no parser ambiguity) from the captured commands — excluding a random Temp EXE from Defender is a near-unambiguous evasion signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin scripting a legitimate AV exclusion for a known dev tool in Temp (rare and usually for Program Files, not Temp)
  • Endpoint management tooling adding temporary exclusions during software deployment
  • Security testers validating Defender exclusion behavior
  • Installer routines that whitelist their own temp extractor
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (" ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the excluded EXE path/name and check whether that file exists and its prevalence (DeviceFileEvents) — a randomly-named Temp EXE is the tell. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the exclusion (Remove-MpPreference), quarantine the Temp EXE, and run a full scan. 3) Hunt: review all Add-MpPreference exclusions across the fleet for Temp/AppData targets and correlate with the Node.js implant (UC3) and relauncher (UC4) on the same device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-ExclusionProcess"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "powershell.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-ExclusionProcess"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js implant C2 beacon to safedocphoto/recallnine/kentjerk/photodoc-secure .info domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution and outbound connections to the campaign's named .info C2 domains, especially when initiated by node.exe over non-standard ports. Article-specific because the four .info domains are confirmed C2 IOCs passed as node.exe arguments. Rationale: Anchored on the four article-confirmed C2 domains plus the discriminator that node.exe is the initiating process — node.exe reaching arbitrary .info hosts on non-standard ports is the campaign's beacon signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1571/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sinkhole or threat-intel scanners resolving the same .info domains for research
  • Security tooling proactively resolving IOCs for blocklisting
  • A legitimate internal Node service that coincidentally talks to a .info domain (the named domains make this near-zero)
  • DNS logging of a passive resolver pre-caching the domains
Suppression filter
| where RemotePort !in (80, 443) or RemoteUrl has_any ("safedocphoto.info","recallnine.info","kentjerk.info","photodoc-secure.info")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving/connecting process is node.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs and note the RemotePort (non-standard ports raise confidence). 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the four .info domains and their resolved IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and kill the node.exe tree. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS and proxy logs org-wide for the four domains and any sibling .cfd/.info infrastructure, and correlate hits to the implant execution (UC3) and Defender exclusion (UC5).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("safedocphoto.info","recallnine.info","kentjerk.info","photodoc-secure.info") or RemoteUrl endswith ".info"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery in~ ("safedocphoto.info","recallnine.info","kentjerk.info","photodoc-secure.info")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CL-STA-1062 Targets Southeast Asian Governments and Critical Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% · [LLM] Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure · [LLM] SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 TinyRCT .NET backdoor, which masquerades as Visual Studio's PerfWatson2.exe but enforces an environment check that it runs only from %LOCALAPPDATA%. Legitimate PerfWatson2.exe ships inside the Visual Studio install tree under Program Files, so any PerfWatson2.exe launching from AppData\Local is article-specific TinyRCT behaviour. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade name PerfWatson2.exe plus TinyRCT's own self-imposed %LOCALAPPDATA% execution constraint; legitimate PerfWatson2 lives under Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio, making AppData\Local execution near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable/extracted copy of Visual Studio components from a profile folder
  • Visual Studio installer caching PerfWatson2 in AppData during an update (rare, usually Program Files)
  • Security tooling copying the binary to AppData for analysis on an analyst workstation
  • EDR sandbox detonation copying the sample into LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and not(FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft PerfWatson2 (legit is signed 'Microsoft Corporation' under Program Files). Check the parent process and whether the host concurrently beaconed to 45.32.113.172 or 139.180.134.221. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the AppData\Local copy; block both C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the environment for any PerfWatson2.exe outside Program Files, for the GoogleUpdater scheduled task, and for choice.exe-based self-delete batch chains indicating TinyRCT cleanup.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\PerfWatson2.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two confirmed CL-STA-1062 IPs: 45.32.113.172 (TinyRCT HTTP C2, ~10s beacon) and 139.180.134.221 (payload/tool-staging server hosting the PerfWatson2.exe backdoor and RAR tool archives). Pure-IOC network detection for both beaconing and payload pull. Rationale: Both IPs are explicitly named in the article (139.180.134.221 hosting PerfWatson2.exe; 45.32.113.172 as TinyRCT C2 in the kill-chain block) and confirmed across the Unit 42 report and Talos UAT-7237 overlap; raw IOC hits are high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation services probing the IPs from a corporate range
  • Shared Vultr/cloud hosting reassigning the IP to a benign tenant after takedown (verify timestamps against report publication)
  • Internal vuln scanner configured to crawl flagged IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; if it is PerfWatson2.exe, a fake vmtools.exe, or curl.exe from a web-server context, treat as confirmed. Note beacon cadence (~10s = TinyRCT). 2) Contain: block both IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the source host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on src_ip for prior 139.180.134.221 downloads (RAR/SoftEther tool pulls), and sweep all hosts for second-stage payloads delivered from the staging server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's habit of disguising tunneling tools (SoftEther VPN, VNT) as VMware system binaries such as vmtools.exe. Flags processes named vmtools/vmtoolsd whose signing company is not 'VMware, Inc.' or whose product string references SoftEther — i.e. a VMware-named binary that isn't VMware. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Figure 6/7 masquerade (SoftEther disguised as vmtools.exe, VNT disguised as a VMware executable); the company-name/path mismatch separates the tunneler from genuine VMware Tools without needing a hash. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools where version metadata is stripped/empty after repackaging by an MSP
  • Older VMware Tools builds signed under a legacy company string ('VMware, Inc.' variations)
  • Third-party VM management tools legitimately named vmtools running from a non-standard path
  • Software-distribution systems staging VMware Tools in a temp folder before install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\VMware\VMware Tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the binary's digital signature and the command line for SoftEther/VNT tunnel arguments (server address, listen port). Confirm it isn't VMware-signed. 2) Contain: terminate the tunneler, isolate the host, and block its configured remote VPN/relay endpoint. 3) Hunt: look for scheduled tasks launching the same disguised binary, RDP sessions riding the tunnel, and the same masquerade name on peer hosts indicating lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "VMware, Inc." or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "SoftEther"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileCompany != "VMware, Inc." or ActingProcessFileProduct has "SoftEther"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 establishing persistence via schtasks.exe creating a task named GoogleUpdater (TinyRCT loader) or a task launching a tunneler disguised as vmtools/VNT (Figure 7). Pivots on the task-creation command line rather than the binary itself. Rationale: Combines the article/kill-chain GoogleUpdater task name (TinyRCT loader) with the Figure 7 VNT-as-VMware scheduled task; task creation referencing these masquerade tokens is far more specific than generic schtasks alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Chrome/Updater creating GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore tasks (note: name differs from 'GoogleUpdater')
  • VMware Tools installer registering a legitimate vmtools-related task
  • Admin scripts re-creating VMware service tasks during template provisioning
  • Software-packaging tools that template task names containing 'vmtools'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\VMware\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (the binary path and arguments the task launches) and verify whether it points to a signed Google/VMware binary in its standard location. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks across the fleet for the same name/binary, and correlate the task creator process — if it was a web shell (w3wp.exe) or PerfWatson2.exe, escalate to full IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command-execution channel where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/curl/rar and native recon binaries — the actor piped system/network enumeration to actor IPs via curl and staged source code into RAR archives directly from the web shell. Rationale: Encodes the article's web-shell-as-execution-mechanism (Figure 4 curl enumeration, Figure 2 source-code archiving) via the w3wp.exe parent pivot — IIS workers should virtually never spawn curl, rar, tracert, or whoami. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web applications shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • Application deployment scripts invoking cmd.exe under the app pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that run ipconfig/netstat from a web context
  • Developer health-check endpoints that exec systeminfo
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck", "\\Monitoring\\") and FileName in~ ("ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command lines — recon piped to curl targeting 45.32.113.172/139.180.134.221 or rar with -hp confirms malicious use; review IIS logs for the requesting URI and source IP (the web shell). 2) Contain: pull the offending .aspx file, isolate the web server, and reset the app-pool service account credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate recently written/modified .aspx files in web roots, and pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing servers for the same web-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe", "httpd.exe", "php-cgi.exe", "tomcat.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "curl.exe", "rar.exe", "whoami.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "tracert.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "netstat.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\rar.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\tracert.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\netstat.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's data-staging step: compressing findings (MSSQL dumps, entire web-server source-code directories) into header-encrypted, password-protected RAR archives using the rar -hp flag prior to exfil. Pivots on the -hp<password> add-to-archive command line, which survives binary renaming. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit tradecraft of compressing findings into password-protected RAR archives; the -hp<password> token (header encryption with an inline password) is rarely used by legitimate users and is the actor's recurring staging signature. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins archiving log bundles or backups with a password for transport
  • Legitimate use of WinRAR with -hp by a power user securing personal data
  • Backup software that wraps RAR with header encryption
  • Developers packaging release artifacts with a protected archive
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Backup\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the archive path and contents source — large archives built from web roots, database export folders, or user document trees signal staging. Check which process invoked rar (web shell = high severity). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive, and watch for immediate outbound transfer to the actor IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the archive creation time with subsequent curl/POST egress and SoftEther tunnel activity; sweep peer hosts for the same -hp pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where ProcessCommandLine has " a "
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where CommandLine has " a "
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
